summary: A news feature on a fictional-seeming global wave of volcanic eruptions starting September 15, 2023 with Mount Eldflaug, producing a "volcanic winter" or "Ashen Plague" that dims skies and cools climates. It covers the International Volcanic Research Coalition's investigation into tectonic shifts and climate change as possible causes, and expert warnings about impacts on agriculture, tourism, air travel and health.
one_line: Simultaneous global volcanic eruptions since September 2023 cause a volcanic winter, prompting scientific inquiry into tectonic and climate causes and warnings about food, tourism and health impacts.
key_facts: Mount Eldflaug erupted without warning on September 15, 2023, starting the series of eruptions described as the "Ashen Plague".
Within a week, volcanoes on other continents followed, including Mt. Akan in Japan, Mount Merapi in Indonesia, and Popocatépetl in Mexico, sending ash plumes into the stratosphere.
Farmer Ásta Jónsdóttir described the horizon at Eldflaug as split in two, one side blue and the other smeared with ashes over the sun.
The International Volcanic Research Coalition (IVRC) was formed of geologists, climatologists and vulcanologists to investigate the eruptions.
Dr. Emma Harrow said in a December 3, 2023 interview that the simultaneity of the eruptions is perplexing and suggests an underlying pattern, a "cadence to the chaos".
Geophysicist Dr. Daiki Tanaka reported an uptick in subterranean movement not seen in the modern age, possibly destabilizing magmatic chambers beneath volcanoes.
Climatologist Dr. Nadia Patel argues that melting ice and rising seas could shift pressure on the Earth's crust and trigger volcanic activity.
Atmospheric physicist Dr. Anthony Rivera said at a November 8, 2023 conference that atmospheric circulation is spreading volcanic particles far from their origins, affecting air quality and weather.
Satellite imagery and high-altitude weather balloons are being used to track the spread of ash and particulates.
Agricultural scientist Dr. Aileen Zhou warned that crops cannot photosynthesize properly under dimmed conditions and a cooler climate shortens the growing season.
Tourism analyst Mark Fitzgerald said the tourism sector is hit hard and the world is on the brink of a recession as travelers cancel plans.
The eruptions threaten agricultural yields, air travel and respiratory health, and highlight disparities in disaster preparedness and response.
